title: SHE CROSSED THE EARTH WITH QUESTIONS—THEN JESUS REVEALED WHY HER JOURNEY STILL MATTERS
paragraphs: SHE CROSSED THE EARTH WITH QUESTIONS—THEN JESUS REVEALED WHY HER JOURNEY STILL MATTERS

The Queen of Sheba came carrying gold, spices, and questions. But what took her breath away was something money could never purchase—and centuries later, Jesus Christ used her journey to confront every soul that keeps asking questions while refusing to come to the Truth.
She had everything powerful people are supposed to have.
Wealth.
Influence.
An entourage large enough to announce her importance before she ever spoke a word.

Camels moved toward Jerusalem carrying spices, enormous quantities of gold, and precious stones. Servants traveled with her. Resources surrounded her. Somewhere behind the royal appearance stood a woman accustomed to entering rooms where other people lowered their heads.
But she was traveling because there was something all her wealth could not give her.
Answers.
And perhaps that is where her story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because you can have money and still lie awake wondering why your heart feels empty.
You can have people admiring you and secretly wonder whether anybody actually knows you.
You can smile in church while carrying questions you are afraid to say aloud.
You can quote Scripture while privately wrestling with disappointment.
You can believe God exists and still whisper in the darkness:
“Lord... where are You?”
“Why did You allow this?”
“Why didn't You answer me?”
“Why am I still fighting the same temptation?”
“Why did they leave?”
“Why did I lose what I prayed so desperately to keep?”
“Can You forgive what I have done?”
“Can someone like me really begin again?”
The Bible does not introduce the Queen of Sheba as a woman without questions.
It introduces her as a woman willing to travel with them.
And that changes everything.
The Hebrew text of 1 Kings 10:1 says:
“וּמַלְכַּת־שְׁבָא שֹׁמַעַת אֶת־שֵׁמַע שְׁלֹמֹה לְשֵׁם יְהוָה וַתָּבֹא לְנַסֹּתוֹ בְּחִידוֹת”
U-malkat Sheva shoma'at et-shema Shelomoh... vattavo lenassoto beḥidot.
The final word matters:
בְּחִידוֹת — beḥidot.
It is the plural of ḥidah and can refer to riddles, enigmas, difficult or perplexing questions.
She did not travel all that distance for small talk.
She came to test Solomon.
She had heard about his extraordinary wisdom in connection with the name of the LORD, and she wanted to discover whether what she had heard could survive examination.
That is important because biblical faith is not presented here as terror of sincere questions.
The woman came questioning.
She came testing.
She came searching.
And Scripture does not hide it.
But then 1 Kings 10:2 gives us a sentence that may be even more beautiful:
She spoke to Solomon about all that was in her heart.
Not merely politics.
Not merely philosophy.
Not merely royal trivia.
Her heart entered the conversation.
That is where some of us stop.
We will bring God our church vocabulary.
We will bring Him our Sunday clothes.
We will bring Him carefully edited prayers.
We will bring Him the version of ourselves we think Christians are supposed to display.
But we are terrified to bring Him what is actually in our hearts.
The resentment.
The lust.
The envy.
The doubt.
The grief.
The secret habit.
The anger toward someone who hurt us.
The disappointment with God that we would never dare admit publicly.
The shame attached to something we did years ago.
The question we think a “good Christian” should have stopped asking by now.
So we polish the outside while something inside us is bleeding.
The Queen of Sheba arrived with treasure...
but she also arrived with questions.
Maybe you need to hear this today:
Stop pretending before God.
He already knows.
The God who sees your public worship also sees the private war.
The God who hears the prayer you speak aloud also knows the sentence you were too ashamed to finish.
You do not shock an omniscient God by finally telling Him the truth.
Bring Him what is in your heart.
But there is another side to this story, and we must not miss it.
The Queen did not merely want her skepticism protected.
She was willing to have her assumptions overturned.
That is the difference between searching for truth and merely searching for arguments that protect what we already want to believe.
She traveled.
She listened.
She observed.
She tested.
Then she allowed the evidence before her to change what she believed.
Solomon answered her questions. She saw his wisdom, his house, his table, his servants, their order and attire, and his relationship to the worship of the LORD.
Then Scripture gives us an extraordinary Hebrew expression:
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ
ve-lo hayah vah od ruaḥ.
Literally, there was no more ruaḥ—breath, wind, spirit—in her.
She was overwhelmed.
Breathless.
The woman who arrived prepared to examine Solomon found herself stunned by what she encountered.
Then something beautiful happened.
Her amazement did not terminate on Solomon.
She said:
“Blessed be the LORD your God.”
That matters.
Because Solomon's wisdom was never supposed to make Solomon the ultimate object of worship.
The gift was supposed to point beyond the gifted man to the Giver.

She recognized that Solomon's throne and wisdom existed within the LORD's purposes for Israel, and 1 Kings 10:9 connects his kingship with God's enduring love for Israel and with the responsibility to practice justice and righteousness.
And here the story could end beautifully.
A foreign queen hears.
She travels.
She questions.
She sees.
She becomes overwhelmed.
She blesses the LORD.
But Jesus refused to let the story remain safely buried in Israel's history.
Centuries passed.
Solomon died.
His magnificent kingdom fractured.
The gold lost its shine.
The palace could not preserve him.
And Solomon himself, despite extraordinary God-given wisdom, was still a fallen man. Scripture later records the tragedy of his heart being turned away through his loves and compromises.
Human wisdom had shown its limit.
Human kingship had shown its limit.
Human glory had shown its limit.
Then Jesus came.
And suddenly the Queen of Sheba's journey became far more than an ancient royal visit.
Jesus Himself reached back into this story.
In Matthew 12:42 He spoke about the Queen of the South coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Then He said words that completely change how Christians must read this story:
“καὶ ἰδοὺ πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε.”
Kai idou pleion Solomōnos hōde.
“And behold, something greater than Solomon is here.”
Greater than Solomon.
Jesus did not point His hearers backward and say, “If only Solomon were still here.”
He pointed to Himself.
Solomon possessed wisdom given by God.
Christ is greater than Solomon.
Solomon sat upon Israel's throne for a season.
Christ is the promised Son of David whose kingdom reaches beyond the temporary splendor of an earthly palace.
Solomon could answer extraordinary questions.
Jesus answers humanity's deepest catastrophe.
Sin.
Guilt.
Alienation from God.
Judgment.
Death.
Solomon could tell a queen what she did not know.
Jesus came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where the story stops being comfortable.
Because Jesus' reference to the Queen of the South was not merely admiration.
It was a warning.
She traveled from far away because she heard there was wisdom in Jerusalem.
Yet the people standing before Jesus had Someone greater than Solomon in their midst.
She moved toward the light she had received.
They were in danger of rejecting greater light standing directly before them.
Think about that.
She traveled an enormous distance to hear Solomon.
Some of us will not cross the distance between our pride and repentance to come to Christ.
She brought difficult questions.
We sometimes use difficult questions as barricades.
She investigated what she heard.
She admitted that what she had heard was not even half of what she discovered.
We sometimes encounter Christ repeatedly and remain determined to keep Him at a safe religious distance.
That is the knife-edge of this story.
Your questions are not necessarily the greatest danger to your soul.
Sometimes the greater danger is deciding beforehand that no answer will ever be allowed to change you.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus, I don't understand—teach me,” and saying, “Jesus, I will only follow You if You agree with everything I have already decided.”
One is the posture of a disciple.
The other tries to put God on trial while refusing to let God examine us.
And eventually the questions turn around.
You came asking whether Christianity is true.
But sooner or later Christ confronts you with another question:
What will you do with Me?
You came asking why the world is broken.
Christ begins exposing the brokenness inside your own heart.
You came asking why people are hypocrites.
Christ asks what you have been hiding.
You came asking why God allows evil.
Then His holiness forces you to confront the evil you have excused when it benefited you.
You came looking for an argument.
You discovered a mirror.
And suddenly...
there is no more breath in you.
Because the Gospel does something human pride hates.
It tells us that our deepest problem is not merely ignorance.
We are sinners in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
We cannot purchase our innocence.
We cannot outperform our guilt.
We cannot decorate our way into heaven.
We cannot carry enough gold into Jerusalem to ransom our own souls.
But this is exactly where scandal becomes grace.
Because the King greater than Solomon did something Solomon never could.
Jesus did not merely sit upon a throne waiting for broken people to make the journey to Him.
He came for us.
The eternal Son entered our humanity.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He received the rejected.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
And then the innocent Christ went to the cross.
The King wore thorns.
The righteous One was treated as condemned.
The sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
The One greater than Solomon did not simply answer our difficult questions.
He carried our guilt.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was insignificant.
And grace did not mean that holiness disappeared.
Christ bore sin's judgment so that forgiveness could be offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Then death itself received a question it could not answer.
The tomb received Jesus...
and could not keep Him.
He rose.
That is Christianity's staggering announcement.
Not “become slightly more religious.”
Not “clean yourself up enough for God to tolerate you.”
Not “hide your scandal carefully so church people never discover it.”
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Receive grace.
Be forgiven.
Be made new.
The Queen of Sheba brought Solomon what was in her heart.
What would happen if tonight you finally brought Jesus what is in yours?
Not the edited version.
Everything.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I have doubts.”
“Jesus, I am addicted.”
“Jesus, I have been pretending.”
“Jesus, I don't know how to repair what I destroyed.”
“Jesus, I am tired of hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are people reading these words who have mastered appearing fine.
Your family thinks you're fine.
Your Facebook friends think you're fine.
People at church think you're fine.
Maybe even your spouse thinks you're fine.
But you know what happens when the room gets quiet.
You know the memory.
You know the browser history.
You know the bitterness.
You know the compromise.
You know the prayer you stopped praying because hope became painful.
And Christ knows too.
Yet the Gospel invitation remains.
Come.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Come because Christ is sufficient for sinners who repent and trust Him.
Maybe your hardest question was never, “Can God explain everything to me?”
Maybe it was:
“After everything I have done, would Jesus still receive me?”
Look toward the cross.
That is where Christianity tells you to search for the answer.
The Gospel is not the story of impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the announcement that God acted in Christ to save sinners who could never save themselves.
So bring your questions.
But bring your heart too.
Bring your doubts.
But bring your willingness to surrender when truth confronts you.
Bring your wounds.
Bring your failures.
Bring your secret history.
Bring the chapter you wish could be ripped from your story.
Jesus is greater than Solomon.
And He is not merely offering you information.
He calls you to Himself.
We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, love, worship, generosity, and witness.
Do not keep every Gospel resource inside the walls of people who already agree with you.
Let the searching person see it.
Let the exhausted believer see it.
Let the person who hasn't entered a church for years see it.
Let the person carrying shame see it.
Let the skeptic with difficult questions see it.
Let the lukewarm Christian see it.
Let someone discover that Christianity is not frightened by honest questions—and that ultimately the Christian hope is not found in Solomon's wisdom, but in Jesus Christ.
It is simply a practical way to support Gospel Warrior's continued work while receiving deeper discipleship content, biblical nourishment, spiritual sharpening, encouragement, and accountability.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous before God.
Perhaps they have gold in their hands but emptiness in their heart.
Perhaps they look successful while privately falling apart.
Perhaps they have spent years testing Christianity from a distance.
Perhaps they are waiting for permission to bring everything in their heart before Jesus.
The Queen of Sheba traveled from the ends of the earth because she heard about the wisdom of Solomon.
You do not need a caravan.
You do not need camels carrying gold.
You do not need precious stones.
You do not need to become respectable enough to approach Christ.
You need to come.
And when you come, remember the words of Jesus:
Someone greater than Solomon is here.
Your questions may have started the journey.
But Jesus is the destination.
And maybe the greatest surprise awaiting you is not that Christ can answer every question you carry...
but that while you were searching for answers, the Savior was exposing the deeper question of your heart:
Will you trust Me?
Bring Him what is in your heart.
Even the scandal.
Especially the scandal.
Because the cross declares that your darkest chapter does not have to be the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.

You may have come carrying a thousand questions—but when you truly encounter the King greater than Solomon, the question that follows you home is whether you can ever again live as though you never met Him.
